# SQL Server

Microsoft's relational engine, driven here as **T-SQL on SQL Server 2019** across seven annotated
scripts in [[data-warehousing-and-business-intelligence]] — two analytics labs, a star-schema
DDL/ETL pair, and a three-script pipeline for the price mart.

## The analytics surface

`sql/01_analytics/` is a tour of the reporting operators the engine provides and portable SQL does
not: `PIVOT` for months-across-years-down crosstabs, `ROLLUP` and `GROUPING SETS` for subtotal rows,
`GROUPING()` to tell a subtotal `NULL` apart from a data `NULL`, `CASE` banding, and `ROW_NUMBER`
for profiling. These are the operators that make a BI query one statement instead of a union of
five.

## Locale is a correctness problem, not a display problem

Two comments in the repo make the same point about the same class of bug — functions whose output
depends on server configuration rather than on the data:

- `DATENAME(MONTH, ...)` returns the session language's month name, so a `PIVOT` whose `IN` list is
  a set of English literals silently produces all-`NULL` columns on a differently configured server.
  The fix used is `CHOOSE(MONTH(...), 'January', ...)` — an explicit mapping.
- `DATEPART(WEEKDAY, ...)` depends on `SET DATEFIRST`.

> "DATEPART(WEEKDAY) depends on SET DATEFIRST, which varies by server language. This form is
> absolute: 1 = Monday, 7 = Sunday, everywhere."
> — Data-Warehousing-and-Business-Intelligence/sql/02_star_schema/02_load_star_schema.sql, 2026-07-25

The replacement is `(DATEDIFF(DAY, '19000101', d.[Date]) % 7) + 1` — arithmetic on a fixed epoch,
which no session setting can move. Both fixes trade a readable builtin for a form whose result is a
function of the input alone.

## Types chosen against the default

Prices are `DECIMAL(18, 6)`, never `FLOAT`, and the reason is written down: binary floating point
cannot represent a decimal price exactly, so sums drift and equality comparisons stop being
reliable. The AdventureWorks fact carries `DECIMAL(19,4)` money columns and a `DECIMAL(38,6)` line
total for the same reason. `DailyRange AS (High - Low) PERSISTED` is a computed column materialised
on write — derived data that cannot drift out of sync with its inputs.

## `ISNULL`, not `DEFAULT`

> "ISNULL, not the column DEFAULT. A DEFAULT applies only when no value is supplied; selecting an
> explicit NULL into the column bypasses it, so the declared 'Unknown' would never take effect."
> — Data-Warehousing-and-Business-Intelligence/sql/02_star_schema/02_load_star_schema.sql, 2026-07-25

A `DEFAULT` constraint is a property of the *insert statement*, not of the column. An ETL that
projects a source column straight into the target never triggers it. This is the kind of thing that
looks fine in a schema review and produces a dimension full of nulls in production.

## Other engine features leaned on

`OUTER APPLY` to pull one correlated row per customer (a primary address) without a window function
or a subquery-in-select. `IDENTITY(1,1)` for the repo's single true surrogate key — see
[[surrogate-vs-natural-keys]]. Window frames with `ROWS BETWEEN 13 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` carry
the whole moving-average indicator: [[window-function-frames]] and [[relative-strength-index]].
Foreign keys and `CHECK` constraints are declared and relied on rather than enforced in application
code — see [[verify-the-load-dont-declare-it]].

## The cost

SQL Server is the heaviest environment in the source set. Running any of this needs a live SQL
Server 2019 instance with both `AdventureWorks2019` and `AdventureWorksDW2019` attached, plus SQL
Server Data Tools for the [[ssis]] and [[ssas]] projects. Nothing in the repo executes on a clean
clone, and no query output is committed. That is precisely why the price indicator was re-expressed
in Python over [[sqlite]] as a runnable specification —
{{reference-implementation-as-specification}} — and it is the sharpest contrast in the source set
with [[zero-dependency-no-build-step]].
